content: Abelmoschus moschatus, also known by various names such as Ambrette seeds, Annual hibiscus, Musk mallow, and Tropical jewel hibiscus, is an aromatic and medicinal plant belonging to the Malvaceae family. It is native to India. The seeds of this plant emit a sweet, floral, and musky fragrance. Despite its tropical origin, the plant is resistant to frost. Historically, musk mallow oil was used as a substitute for animal musk, but this practice has largely been discontinued due to its potential to cause photosensitivity. The plant has numerous culinary applications. Its seeds are sometimes added to coffee, while the unripe pods (referred to as musk okra), leaves, and young shoots are consumed as vegetables. Various parts of the plant are utilized in traditional and complementary medicine, although not all of these uses have been scientifically validated. Externally, it is applied to alleviate digestive spasms, cramps, poor circulation, and joint pain. Additionally, it is considered to have insecticidal properties and is believed to act as an aphrodisiac. In industrial applications, the mucilage from its roots is used for sizing paper, and its flowers are occasionally used to flavor tobacco. The cultivation of this medicinal crop, known as Kasturi Bhindi in India, is gaining popularity among small-scale farmers. Initially, growers were hesitant to cultivate it due to its susceptibility to insect infestations. However, with experience and improved practices, farmers have become more confident in its cultivation. Unlike other medicinal crops, the focus has shifted from merely producing planting material to serious efforts in high-quality production, with the aim of extracting oil for the international market. Kasturi Bhindi is particularly valued for its aromatic seeds, which possess a distinctive musky scent. In trade, it is commonly referred to as Ambrette. While its various plant parts are used in traditional medicine and herbal formulations, the demand for this plant extends beyond traditional healers to national and international markets. Farmers, however, are not primarily cultivating it for traditional healers, who instead rely on wild populations and small-scale cultivation to meet their needs.
